comparator.name: Griekse en Latijnse Taal en Cultuur (Greek and Latin Languages and Cultures)
comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 (Onderwijs- en Examenregeling, the formally adopted regulation for the Fall 2026 intake)
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme is taught in Dutch and delivered within the ACASA partnership between VU and the University of Amsterdam, with teaching on the UvA campus. Articles 11.1, 11.3, 11.4 and 12.1 of the formally adopted 2026-2027 OER establish the complete 180-EC pathway: a 60-EC propedeuse of ten compulsory 6-EC units, 78 EC of compulsory post-propedeutic units, 30 EC of genuine free elective space in the third year and a 12-EC bachelor thesis including its colloquium. The OER contains no formal routes, tracks or specializations, so no route is selected and the elective space is preserved generically rather than filled with invented content. The zero-credit faculty language test (VU_TAALTOETS) remains compulsory but carries no EC and is therefore outside the 180-EC component list. One discrepancy was found and resolved in favour of the formally adopted source: the recruitment page lists Griekse en Latijnse Komedie among the third-year subjects, but the OER programme schedule marks that unit (L_AABAGLT309, 6 EC) with an asterisk as an additional elective module and omits it from the compulsory list in article 11.4, so it is not presented as compulsory here. Bijlage 2 of the OER describes a shortened programme for students entering after another UvA humanities propedeuse; it is not the standard pathway and was not used.

alternatives.label: Classical antiquity through literature, rhetoric, philosophy and archaeology
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to a Greek and Latin degree: the literature, myth, rhetoric, philosophy, cultural history and material remains of Greek and Roman antiquity, studied together with the reception of antiquity in later periods, and with close textual and stylistic analysis as its central method. UCR teaches no ancient Greek or Latin, so this programme studies the classical world and its afterlife in translation and through its material and historical evidence rather than reproducing the VU language curriculum.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum divides roughly evenly between literary studies, rhetoric and stylistics, philosophy, and the cultural history, archaeology and reception of antiquity, so the label names that combination instead of presenting it as a classics or a literature degree; it deliberately does not claim Greek or Latin, which the programme does not contain.
progression: Introductory literary studies, classical rhetoric, Western philosophy and world archaeology are placed in the first year, before the 200-level work on Greek archaeology, stylistics, myth and epic, empires and ancient warfare, and before the third-year courses on ancient democratic heritage, persuasive communication, adaptation, interpretive theory, art-historical research and the archival research seminar. No scheduled course carries a formal prerequisite, every course is offered in its assigned term, and the one 100-level course placed in year two, Introduction to Western Art History, is a deliberate entry point into the Renaissance reception strand rather than a displaced foundation.

alternatives.label: Antiquity, democracy and the politics of the present
alternatives.concept: A question-led programme built on the VU programme's own claim that antiquity helps us think about present-day questions: it studies how ancient communities organised democracy, citizenship, membership, empire and mobility, and then examines the modern political, legal and social orders in which those ancient arrangements are still invoked. Its organising method is comparative political, legal and historical analysis rather than textual and literary interpretation.
alternatives.labelReason: The finished curriculum contains four ancient-world courses and a substantial block of law, comparative politics, international relations and modern history, so the label names both the ancient starting point and the present-day political and legal material that dominates years two and three, rather than presenting the programme as ancient history.
progression: Law, Society & Justice, political philosophy and Western philosophy open the first year and Law, Society & Justice precedes every law course that formally requires it. World archaeology, Greek archaeology, public international law and ethics follow in semester two; comparative politics, modern history, empires and human rights in semester three; and the 300-level work on private law, EU politics, ancient democratic heritage, peace and conflict, EU law, historical research and art-historical research in years three. Every formal prerequisite is completed earlier and every course is offered in its assigned term.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 organises the field around texts: it asks how classical literature, rhetoric and philosophy work and how they were later rewritten, and its method is close reading, stylistic analysis and interpretation. Alternative 2 starts from the VU programme's own question about what Roman and Greek arrangements for citizenship, migration and democracy mean today, and answers it with comparative political, legal and historical analysis. That difference is not a relabelling: twelve of the twenty-four courses differ, the entire literature, rhetoric and creative-writing block of Alternative 1 is absent, and it is replaced by a coherent legal and political sequence running from Law, Society & Justice through public international law, comparative constitutional law, private law and EU law to comparative politics, international relations, EU politics and peace and conflict, with modern history supplying the period in which classical models were invoked.
traceOverrides: examines how Western thinkers from the classical political philosophers onward theorised political authority and the good community, which is the question this programme carries into the present
studies the archaeology of community and collective decision-making in early-democratic Greece, giving this programme its material evidence for how an ancient democracy actually worked

reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built, how ancient commentators attacked it as too inclusive and too emotional, and how that contested heritage has been reused since, which is this programme's central case
examines how empires rise, hold and lose power, placing Rome alongside later imperial formations that invoked it
reads ancient myth and epic comparatively and follows how those narratives were carried into later cultures that used them to explain their own political order
trains archival and primary-source historical research, the method this programme uses to test claims about how the past is invoked in present-day argument

selection.assessment: Two UCR alternatives are defensible and a third is not. Alternative 1 is the closest feasible response to a Greek and Latin degree that UCR can build: it reproduces the literary, rhetorical, philosophical, cultural-historical and reception strands of the VU programme but cannot reproduce its core, because UCR teaches neither Greek nor Latin and offers no linguistics of either language. Alternative 2 follows the VU programme's own explicit claim that antiquity illuminates present-day questions about democracy, citizenship and migration, and turns it into a comparative political, legal and historical programme; it differs from Alternative 1 in twelve of twenty-four courses and in its organising method. A third candidate, classical reception and creative rewriting, was tested and rejected as not substantively distinct: its evidence is already carried by Alternative 1, which contains Renaissance Italy and the global Mediterranean, Western art history, film and text, and the creative communication laboratory, and no genuinely different 24-course curriculum follows from it without arbitrary substitutions. A fourth candidate, teaching and transmitting Greek and Latin, was rejected as not feasible: UCR has neither the classical languages nor a teacher-education curriculum, so no coherent 24-course programme could be built for it. No alternative was manufactured to reach three.

blocks: Greek and Latin language and linguistic analysis

UCR teaches no ancient Greek. No scheduled UCR course delivers Greek language acquisition or the reading of Greek texts in the original, so this row stays blank rather than being filled with a course about language in general.
UCR teaches no Latin. No scheduled UCR course delivers Latin language acquisition or the reading of Latin texts in the original.
This second language-acquisition course continues reading in the original Greek and Latin; UCR offers no equivalent.

This course acquires further Greek and Latin through philosophical and rhetorical prose. UCR's rhetoric courses treat classical rhetorical theory, but they do not teach the languages this component is built on, so no row-level match is asserted.

UCR offers no linguistics of ancient Greek. Its nearest linguistic work, modern stylistics, analyses style in mainly modern texts and is not a counterpart to the historical grammar and linguistics of Greek.
UCR offers no linguistics of Latin, and no scheduled course addresses the historical development or grammar of the Latin language.
Classical literature, myth and literary interpretation

Both survey the canonical literary highlights of the tradition and read them against critical and theoretical texts; the VU course surveys Greek and Latin literature specifically, while the UCR course runs from the ancient world to post-modernity and reads the ancient texts in translation.

Both read Homeric epic and its narrative technique. The VU course studies Homer in Greek as a dedicated epic course, whereas the UCR course reads Homer alongside Virgil and non-European epic traditions in a comparative frame.

Both require an independent, text-based research paper in which the student applies an explicit interpretive framework to primary texts and defends the result; the VU paper is written on a classical subject in the original languages.

Both combine the critical study of how earlier texts and forms are reworked with the student's own creative writing, including work on poetic form; the VU course takes the classical tradition as its material.
UCR has no course on Greek tragedy. Tragedy appears only incidentally within broader literature courses, which is not a sufficient counterpart to a dedicated tragedy course read in Greek.

UCR has no dedicated course on Virgilian epic. Virgil is read comparatively within World Myth & Literature, and that course is already the canonical counterpart of the Greek epic component, so this row stays blank.
UCR offers no study of late-antique and medieval Greek literature.
UCR offers no study of late-antique and medieval Latin literature, and none of its courses addresses the role of Latin in medieval European culture.
UCR has no course on Latin lyric poetry. Its creative-writing laboratory works on lyric form in general and is already placed with the reception and creative-writing component.
Cultural history, material remains and the memory of antiquity

Both introduce the ancient societies of the Near East and the Greek world; the VU course does so as cultural history across the whole region and period, while the UCR course works from material culture and craft production and extends beyond the Mediterranean.

Both treat the formation and extension of Roman power in the Hellenistic and Italian world. The VU course is a cultural history of that period, while the UCR course examines Rome as one case in a comparative history and theory of empires.

Both train students to work directly with primary historical source material and to build a documented argument from it. The VU course does so with the sources for antiquity, whereas the UCR seminar works on an early-nineteenth-century campaign and its archives; the method is shared, the period is not.
Both examine how sites, objects and texts of the classical world became places of memory and how that memory was reused by later societies.

UCR does not read the Greek and Latin historians. Its history courses study modern and comparative historical writing, which is not a counterpart to reading Herodotus, Thucydides, Livy or Tacitus in the original.
UCR has no field excursion to ancient sites and no equivalent supervised study visit within the ancient-world curriculum.
Philosophy, disciplinary reflection and independent research

Both introduce ancient philosophy and its arguments. The VU course is dedicated to antiquity, while the UCR course opens with the ancient Greeks and then continues through the whole Western tradition.

Both reflect on how a humanities discipline constitutes itself: the history of the field, its methods and the writing of scholarship. The VU course does this for the ancient-studies disciplines generally, the UCR course through art history.
UCR's 24 scheduled courses contain no bachelor thesis; the standardized optional independent-research element is shown here in parallel with the VU thesis.

This is genuine free elective space in the VU programme, which the student fills with a minor, free electives, an internship or study abroad. It has no fixed content and therefore no UCR counterpart; the UCR programmes have no separate elective block because every one of their 24 courses is chosen individually.
Politics, law and present-day public questions

notes.text: The Greek and Latin Languages and Cultures programme at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam combines Greek and Latin language acquisition, the linguistics of both languages, and the reading of classical, late-antique and medieval texts in the original. At UCR, students can approach classical antiquity through fields such as literary studies, rhetoric and stylistics, philosophy, ancient and comparative history, archaeology and heritage. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives on the ancient world rather than reproducing a full classics curriculum, and UCR students would not learn to read Greek or Latin.

The VU programme organizes study around a fixed sequence of compulsory Greek and Latin units, with 30 EC of free elective space and a bachelor thesis in the third year. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across individually chosen courses in literature, communication, heritage, philosophy, history, law and politics, and every course carries the same 7.5 EC. The UCR programmes therefore cover related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the external programme course by course, and they contain no separate elective block or thesis; independent research is shown as the standardized optional 15-EC element.
